'''Naomi J. Halas''' is an American physicist and nano scientist. She is University Professor at Rice University and the Stanley C. Moore Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Naomi J. Halas {{!}} Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering (ECE) {{!}} Rice University |url=https://eceweb.rice.edu/naomi-halas |access-date=2020-06-16 |website=eceweb.rice.edu}}</ref> She is also the founding director of Rice University Laboratory for Nanophotonics, and the Smalley-Curl Institute.<ref>{{Cite web |title=SCI Leadership {{!}} Smalley-Curl Institute {{!}} Rice University |url=https://sci.rice.edu/content/sci-leadership |access-date=2020-06-16 |website=sci.rice.edu}}</ref> She invented the first [[nanoparticle]] with tunable [[plasmonic]] resonances, which are controlled by their shape and structure,<ref>{{Cite web |date=25 April 2017 |title=Prof. Naomi Halas {{!}} Women In Science |url=https://www.weizmann.ac.il/WomenInScience/women-science-award/recipients/prof-naomi-halas |access-date=2020-06-27 |website=www.weizmann.ac.il}}</ref> and has won numerous awards for her pioneering work in the field of [[nanophotonics]] and [[plasmonics]]. She was also part of a team that developed the first dark pulse [[soliton]] in 1987 while working for [[IBM]].

Halas was elected a member of the [[National Academy of Engineering]] in 2014 for nanoscale engineering of optical resonances and lineshapes.

She is a Fellow of [[Optica (society)|Optica]], the [[American Physical Society]], the [[International Society for Optical Engineering]] (SPIE), the [[Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers]] (IEEE), the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]]. In 2019, she was named a fellow of the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Halas named a fellow of the Royal Society of Chemistry |url=https://sci.rice.edu/news/halas-named-fellow-royal-society-chemistry |website=[[Rice University]]}}</ref>

Halas was elected a member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 2009, the National Academy of Sciences in 2013, and the [[National Academy of Engineering]] in 2014, the latter for nanoscale engineering of optical resonances and lineshapes. She was elected to the Royal Danish Academy of Sciences and Letters in 2024.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Halas Research Group |url=http://halas.rice.edu/home |access-date=2020-06-27 |website=halas.rice.edu}}</ref>

==Education==
Halas received her bachelor's degree from [[La Salle University]] in 1980. She obtained her master's degree from [[Bryn Mawr College]] in 1984 and her doctorate from Bryn Mawr in 1987.<ref name="auto1">{{Cite web|title=2018 Stanley Corrsin Award Recipient|url=http://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm|access-date=2020-06-27|website=www.aps.org|language=en}}</ref> She was a graduate research fellow at the [[IBM Thomas J Watson Research Center]] during her doctoral studies, during which time she developed the first "dark pulse" [[soliton]] with Dieter Kroekel, Giampiero Giuliani and Daniel Grischkowsky.<ref>{{Cite Q|Q74485347}}</ref> A "dark pulse" soliton is a standing wave that propagates through an [[optical fiber]] without spreading and which consists of a short interruption of a light pulse. She was also part of the first research efforts focusing on time-domain [[terahertz spectroscopy]] during her time at IBM.<ref>{{Cite web|title=AHF Featured Member: Dr. Naomi Halas|url=http://www.americanhungarianfederation.org/featured_naomihalas.htm|access-date=2020-06-27|website=www.americanhungarianfederation.org}}</ref>

== Career ==
Halas conducted her graduate research at the [[IBM]] [[Thomas J. Watson Research Center]] in [[Yorktown Heights, New York]] in the mid-1980s where she worked on ultrafast nonlinear optics and early developments in [[terahertz spectroscopy]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Swearer |first1=Dayne F. |last2=Lal |first2=Surbhi |last3=Large |first3=Nicolas |last4=Manjavacas |first4=Alejandro |title=Tribute to Naomi Halas and Peter Nordlander |journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry C |date=2025 |volume=129 |issue=44 |pages=19683–19684 |doi=10.1021/acs.jpcc.5c06849}}</ref> She subsequently held a postdoctoral appointment at [[AT&T Bell Laboratories]], where her research focused on time-resolved photoemission spectroscopy of semiconductor surfaces.<ref name=":12" />

Halas joined the faculty of Rice University in 1989. Her initial appointment was in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering.<ref name="auto1" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Naomi Halas Ph.D. '87 |url=https://www.brynmawr.edu/bulletin/naomi-halas-phd-87 |access-date=2026-04-02 |website=www.brynmawr.edu |language=en}}</ref>

In 1999 she was appointed professor in electrical and computer engineering and chemistry, and in 2001 she was named the Stanley C. Moore Professor in Electrical and Computer Engineering.<ref name=":12">{{Cite journal |last1=Halas |first1=Naomi J. |title=Autobiography of Naomi Halas |journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry C |date=2025 |volume=129 |issue=44 |pages=19685–19689 |doi=10.1021/acs.jpcc.5c06848}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Biography: Naomi Halas - CNN.com |url=https://www.cnn.com/2007/TECH/science/06/11/halas.biog/ |access-date=2026-04-02 |website=www.cnn.com}}</ref>

In 2004 Halas founded and became director of Rice University’s Laboratory for Nanophotonics, an interdisciplinary research center devoted to the study of light–matter interactions at the nanoscale and their technological applications. She also served as director of the Smalley-Curl Institute.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Thomas |first=Naomi |date=2025-08-22 |title=Franklin Medalist is taking chemistry in new directions |url=https://www.lasalle.edu/news/franklin-medalist-is-taking-chemistry-in-new-directions/ |access-date=2026-04-02 |website=La Salle University}}</ref>

In 2023 she was named University Professor at Rice University, the institution’s highest faculty rank.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-04-14 |title=Rice University professor waits on FDA to approve what she hopes will be a cure for prostate cancer |url=https://abc13.com/post/naomi-halas-rice-university-scientist-stem/11747569/ |access-date=2026-04-02 |website=ABC13 Houston |language=en}}</ref> She became only the tenth person and second woman in the university’s history to receive this title.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Rice, Syzgy Plasmonic's Naomi Halas wins top chemistry honor - Energy Capital |url=https://energycapitalhtx.com/naomi-halas-franklin-medal-chemistry |access-date=2026-04-02 |website=energycapitalhtx.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date= |title=Naomi J. Halas CV |url=https://cpb-us-e1.wpmucdn.com/wordpressua.uark.edu/dist/f/164/files/2017/01/cv_Halas.pdf |access-date=2020-06-27 |website=}}</ref>

== Research ==
Halas is widely recognized for foundational contributions to plasmonics and nanophotonics, particularly the development of tunable plasmonic nanostructures and their application to medicine, sensing, and energy conversion. Her research integrates fundamental physics and chemistry with electromagnetics, nanoscale materials design, and applied photonics technologies.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dr. Naomi Halas {{!}} Advances in Breast Cancer Research Workshop |url=https://wordpressua.uark.edu/breastcancer/dr-naomi-halas/ |access-date=2026-04-02 |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Nanoshells and tunable plasmonic nanostructures ===
Halas is known for inventing plasmon-resonant [[nanoshell]]s, a class of core–shell nanoparticles consisting of a dielectric core (typically silica) coated with a thin metallic shell, usually gold or silver.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Naomi Halas |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/naomi-j-halas-wtmi50/ |access-date=2020-06-27 |website=www.nasonline.org}}</ref> These structures support surface plasmon resonances whose optical response can be precisely controlled by adjusting the relative dimensions of the nanoparticle core and shell.<ref>{{Cite web |title='Nanorice' Created: Could Improve Chemical Sensing, Biological Imaging |url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2006/03/060314231643.htm |access-date=2026-04-02 |website=ScienceDaily |language=en}}</ref>

Her realization of nanoshells demonstrated that optical absorption and scattering could be engineered across a broad spectral range from the visible to the infrared, enabling systematic tuning of light–matter interactions at the nanoscale. This capability provided the first practical implementation of tunable plasmon-resonant nanoparticles, translating theoretical predictions into experimentally controllable optical materials.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Byers |first1=Chad P. |last2=Zhang |first2=Hui |last3=Swearer |first3=Dayne F. |last4=Yorulmaz |first4=Mustafa |last5=Hoener |first5=Benjamin S. |last6=Huang |first6=Da |last7=Hoggard |first7=Anneli |last8=Chang |first8=Wei-Shun |last9=Mulvaney |first9=Paul |last10=Ringe |first10=Emilie |last11=Halas |first11=Naomi J. |last12=Nordlander |first12=Peter |last13=Link |first13=Stephan |last14=Landes |first14=Christy F. |title=From tunable core-shell nanoparticles to plasmonic drawbridges: Active control of nanoparticle optical properties |journal=Science Advances |date=2015 |volume=1 |issue=11 |article-number=e1500988 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.1500988 |pmc=4672758 |pmid=26665175 |bibcode=2015SciA....1E0988B }}</ref>

In 2003, Halas and her colleague [[Jennifer L. West]] were awarded the ''[[Nanotechnology Now]]'' Best Discovery Award for their groundbreaking work to develop a cancer therapy based on metallic nanoshells.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Nanotechnology Now - Best of Nanotechnology - 2003 Awards. Best Discoveries.|url=https://www.nanotech-now.com/2003-Awards/Best-Discoveries-2003.htm|access-date=2020-06-27|website=www.nanotech-now.com}}</ref> Halas also received the Innovator Award from the [[United States Department of Defense|US Department of Defense]] Congressionally Directed Breast Cancer Research Program, and was awarded a four-year $3 million grant to conduct further research into the treatment.<ref name="auto">{{Cite web|title=Halas, West awarded 'best discovery'|url=https://news.rice.edu/2004/02/19/halas-west-awarded-best-discovery/|access-date=2020-06-27|website=news.rice.edu}}</ref>

=== Plasmon hybridization and coupled nanostructures ===
Halas has worked on understanding how plasmonic structures interact when brought together. Her research helped advance the concept of plasmon hybridization, developed with her collaborator [[Peter Nordlander]]. This model compares interacting plasmons in metallic nanostructures to molecular orbitals, showing how their electromagnetic modes combine to form new resonant states.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Nordlander |first1=P. |last2=Oubre |first2=C. |last3=Prodan |first3=E. |last4=Li |first4=K. |last5=Stockman |first5=M. I. |title=Plasmon Hybridization in Nanoparticle Dimers |journal=Nano Letters |date=2004 |volume=4 |issue=5 |pages=899–903 |doi=10.1021/nl049681c |bibcode=2004NanoL...4..899N }}</ref>

The framework explains how factors such as geometry, spacing, and material composition influence optical behavior in nanoparticle assemblies. It has been applied to systems including clusters, nanogaps, and arrays, and has informed the design of tunable plasmonic devices and spectroscopic tools.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Halas |first1=Naomi J. |last2=Lal |first2=Surbhi |last3=Chang |first3=Wei-Shun |last4=Link |first4=Stephan |last5=Nordlander |first5=Peter |title=Plasmons in Strongly Coupled Metallic Nanostructures |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/full/10.1021/cr200061k |journal=Chemical Reviews |pages=3913–3961 |language=en |doi=10.1021/cr200061k |date=8 June 2011 |volume=111 |issue=6 |pmid=21542636 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

=== Surface-enhanced spectroscopy and sensing ===
Halas has developed plasmonic nanostructures for sensitive molecular detection. Nanoshells and related designs can greatly amplify electromagnetic fields, enhancing signals in Raman and infrared spectroscopy.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Herkert |first1=Ediz Kaan |last2=Bermeo Alvaro |first2=Domenica Romina |last3=Recchia |first3=Martina |last4=Langbein |first4=Wolfgang |last5=Borri |first5=Paola |last6=Garcia-Parajo |first6=Maria F. |title=Hybrid Plasmonic Nanostructures for Enhanced Single-Molecule Detection Sensitivity |journal=ACS Nano |date=2023 |volume=17 |issue=9 |pages=8453–8464 |doi=10.1021/acsnano.3c00576 |pmc=10173688 |pmid=37011057 |bibcode=2023ACSNa..17.8453H }}</ref> These effects allow detection of very small amounts of material and support optical nanosensors for identifying chemicals, biomolecules, and environmental toxins.<ref>{{Cite web |title=AHF Featured Member: Dr. Naomi Halas |url=http://www.americanhungarianfederation.org/featured_naomihalas.htm |access-date=2026-04-02 |website=www.americanhungarianfederation.org}}</ref>

=== Photothermal therapy ===
Her initial studies in photothermal cancer therapy were collaborations with bioengineer Professor [[Jennifer L. West|Jennifer West]]. They co-founded a company, Nanospectra Biosciences, which transitioned photothermal cancer therapy into successful clinical trials for prostate cancer.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rastinehad |first1=Ardeshir R. |last2=Anastos |first2=Harry |last3=Wajswol |first3=Ethan |last4=Winoker |first4=Jared S. |last5=Sfakianos |first5=John P. |last6=Doppalapudi |first6=Sai K. |last7=Carrick |first7=Michael R. |last8=Knauer |first8=Cynthia J. |last9=Taouli |first9=Bachir |last10=Lewis |first10=Sara C. |last11=Tewari |first11=Ashutosh K. |last12=Schwartz |first12=Jon A. |last13=Canfield |first13=Steven E. |last14=George |first14=Arvin K. |last15=West |first15=Jennifer L. |last16=Halas |first16=Naomi J. |title=Gold nanoshell-localized photothermal ablation of prostate tumors in a clinical pilot device study |journal=PNAS |date=2019 |volume=116 |issue=37 |pages=18590–18596 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1906929116 |doi-access=free |pmid=31451630 |language=en|pmc=6744844 |bibcode=2019PNAS..11618590R }}</ref>

=== Plasmonic photocatalysis and solar-driven processes ===
Halas has studied the use of plasmonic nanostructures to drive chemical reactions with light. By concentrating electromagnetic energy and generating energetic charge carriers, these materials can enable catalytic processes without conventional heating.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Light-driven chemistry for a sustainable future {{!}} Royal Society |url=https://royalsociety.org/science-events-and-lectures/2026/06/light-driven-chemistry/ |access-date=2026-04-02 |website=royalsociety.org |language=en}}</ref>

Her work showed that reactions such as ammonia cracking and methane reforming can be driven by light. A key concept is the “antenna–reactor” nanoparticle, which combines plasmonic structures with catalytic sites.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Light makes catalyst more effective |url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2018/10/181004143908.htm |access-date=2026-04-02 |website=ScienceDaily |language=en}}</ref>

This research also contributed to the founding of Syzygy Plasmonics, which develops light-driven chemical reactors operating at lower temperatures.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Rice U. technology startup Syzygy Plasmonics raises $76 million in latest funding round |url=https://news.rice.edu/news/2022/rice-u-technology-startup-syzygy-plasmonics-raises-76-million-latest-funding-round |website=[[Rice University]]}}</ref><ref name="publications2">{{Cite web |title=Publications - Halas Research Group |url=http://halas.rice.edu/publications |access-date=2020-06-27 |website=halas.rice.edu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Sivan |first1=Yonatan |last2=Baraban |first2=Joshua |last3=Un |first3=Ieng Wai |last4=Dubi |first4=Yonatan |date=2019-05-03 |title=Comment on "Quantifying hot carrier and thermal contributions in plasmonic photocatalysis" |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aaw9367 |journal=Science |volume=364 |issue=6439 |article-number=eaaw9367 |doi=10.1126/science.aaw9367 |pmid=31048461 |bibcode=2019Sci...364.9367S |url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dubi |first1=Yonatan |last2=Un |first2=Ieng Wai |last3=Baraban |first3=Joshua H. |last4=Sivan |first4=Yonatan |date=April 2022 |title=Distinguishing thermal from non-thermal contributions to plasmonic hydrodefluorination |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41929-022-00767-6 |journal=Nature Catalysis |language=en |volume=5 |issue=4 |pages=244–246 |doi=10.1038/s41929-022-00767-6 |issn=2520-1158 |url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Baffou |first1=Guillaume |last2=Bordacchini |first2=Ivan |last3=Baldi |first3=Andrea |last4=Quidant |first4=Romain |date=2020-06-28 |title=Simple experimental procedures to distinguish photothermal from hot-carrier processes in plasmonics |journal=Light: Science & Applications |language=en |volume=9 |issue=1 |page=108 |doi=10.1038/s41377-020-00345-0  |doi-access=free|pmid=32612818 |issn=2047-7538 |pmc=7321931 |arxiv=2001.08402 |bibcode=2020LSA.....9..108B }}</ref>
